text: https://amzn.to/2Eprf2w —— Nekteck 21W Solar Charger with 2-Port USB Charger Build - High efficiency Solar Panel
Koompi notebook and charger.

Koompi charger, 2 USB chargers (2.1 mA each), extension cord.  The extension cord has a splice (red tape) where I can splice on a different plug for various countries. Often old electronic gadgets can be found, and then cut the cord.

One nice compact tool kit would be better. These heavy items are rarely used so they're at the bottom of my pack. A pedal wrench is needed to remove pedals for flying, and I have a fender wrench and seat wrench.  My smaller tools I carry elsewhere more easily accessable. Chain lubricant, patch cement, patches, and an abrasive. Patch cement in the small metal tubes evaporates or leaks, and will not last long.  I carry my rubber cement in a resealable bottle.

Ground cloth, bivoac sack, silk bag, down bag. This is a very lightweight down bag, but I am still able to keep warm in freezing weather because of layering and other heat saving strategies. The ground cloth and bivoac sack were cut and sewn using a car cover I found in Spain.

Passport, visa photos, various currencies, and three plastic accounts. One account is in the USA, another in Singapore, and another in Cambodia. You must be able to manage your money through the internet.
This is a Topeak Road Morph high pressure pump with a gauge. A very good choice.

I have four stuff bags like this for my tent and fly, clothes and sleeping bags. These are round, which is best, and they're color coded so you know what's in them.  Notice the draw strings are also ties staps, with loop knots on each end. They should be made of rip stop nylon, and have doubles seams to prevent tearing. They don't need to be water proof or even water resistant.

Within the stuff bags are clothes, and now I'll explain about clothes.

Your most important clothes are those you are wearing everyday, because you'll rarely change your clothes, rather you'll just wash and wear again. Most all your clothes should be high quality synthetic stretch material that is both cool and warm, compact, lightweight, durable and quick drying. Wash your clothes one at a time under a water tap or  in a bathroom sink as needed, Wring them out good and dry, then put them on damp to wear.  You may be a bit chilled at first, but you'll find they dry and warm up quickly.

Three very lightweight outer nylon jackets. One is cool, another is a bit warmer and slightly heavier, and the third is a bit more water resistant than the other two.  On very cold nights, I may need to wear all three while in my three sleeping bags.  While riding, daytime temperatures will rarely be so cold as to require needing to wear all your layers.

Here are three shirts, and I am wearing one more, which is a short sleeve. Pictured are two more short sleeve shirts, and one long sleeve shirt. Carry whatever combination you prefer, but four shirts and three jackets is enough for upperwear. They're each synthetic and lightweight, with some heavier others.  They're used for layering during cold days, and especially during cold nights.  I also carry a reflective vest for highway riding.

I am wearing one pair of long pants, and here we see pictured two more pair of long pants. In addition, there is one pair of underwear that serves a double purpose as a swim suit, and there is one pair of short pants.  In the UK, they say trousers.
Helmet and kroma (all purpose towel). Helmet keeps your head cool and the sun out of your eyes, even if you don't strap it down.

Warm, water resistant gloves, knit hat, silk scarf, warm socks, and arm warmers. Each are essential for cold weather. Arm warmers are made from cut off knee socks or you can cut the arms off of an old tight fitting sweater. Every one of these items alone will help you to retain much heat energy. They're all important, because we're carrying no winter clothing. When the cold comes, your equipt to deal with it down to maybe 5 or 10 c below zero. In addition, I am wearing one pair of high quality men's support stockings.

As with most everything else,  your tent should be small, compact, lightweight, durable, and well designed. In this photo my yellow polysil tarp is being used for the rain.  In addition, the blue plastic is being used to keep the bike out of the rain, but such plastic can always be found along the way. I carry a very small and thin sleeping pad which is necessary especially when sleeping on cold earth or cement.
a USB chargeable headlamp is the best choice for an all  purpose work lamp.
Both front and rear lights are wired together with switch on the back of this front lamp. The switched unit then plugs directly into my USB rechargeable external battery pack.
The rear lamp is wired together with the front switched lamp, but this lamp is not mounted well for high visibility. Therefore I have another rear lamp below hanging from my pannier.

This is an ordinary 3 AAA (4.5v) battery head lamp that I found on the trail and decided to keep.  It works well as an auxillary lamp.  It blinks white or red.  You will find many things along the way, so you'll never have worries, only hope.
A ding bell for trail passing.

I believe in high quality all-leather walking shoes with synthetic soles, as well treated leather works well in wet conditions, dries nicely and does not stink.

Cheap clothing and equipment works well for the short term and until you're able to upgrade. Many things can be found alongside the road as you go, or people will give you their hand-me-downs along the way.

In addition, you can't see the Android I'm carrying because it's being used to take the photos. I suppose I could take a photo of it in a mirror, but you get the picture.  All your data should be backed up on the cloud, especially photos of your passport and any other important documents.

 For several of these items above I can offer Amazon affiliate links.

I believe that's everything.
